item.title: Reducing Low-Value Care Through the Smarter Care Virginia Initiative
item.description:
Importance: Low-value care costs more than $100 billion annually and remains pervasive despite decades of evidence documenting its clinical and financial harms. While several US states have begun discouraging its use, the feasibility of such statewide interventions in partnership with large health systems remains unknown.

Objective: To investigate the effectiveness of a clinician-led, multistakeholder, statewide initiative to reduce low-value care in the Commonwealth of Virginia.

Design, setting, and participants: This quality improvement study used a difference-in-differences analyses comparing low-value service changes among patients attributed to 6 health systems vs 12 control systems in the Commonwealth of Virginia preintervention (January 1 to December 31, 2019) vs postintervention (January 1 to December 31, 2022). Any patient eligible to receive 1 or more of the 9 measured low-value services in the 18 health systems evaluated were included. Data were analyzed between December 1, 2023, and September 1, 2026.

Exposure: The intervention, Smarter Care Virginia, included health system financial support, clinician education, and quarterly peer-comparison performance scorecards.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the percentage of patients receiving any of 9 selected low-value services: (1-3) preoperative laboratory, imaging, and cardiac testing; (4-5) electrocardiogram/cardiac screening and cardiac stress testing; (6-7) diagnostic imaging and opioids for acute back pain; (8) advanced diagnostic eye imaging; and (9) peripherally inserted central catheter lines for patients with chronic kidney disease. Secondary outcomes included adverse events (eg, myocardial infarction-related hospitalization) and per-capita spending on the 9 low-value services.

Results: A total of 17 223 clinicians (7222 in the intervention group and 10 001 in the control group) and 4.5 million patients (approximately 68% of Virginia's adult population) were identified. In 2019, 10.5% of patients in the intervention group and 10.7% of patients in the control group received 1 or more low-value services; in 2021 to 2022, rates declined to 8.5% and 9.1%, respectively. The intervention was associated with 10.4% fewer patients receiving 1 or more low-value services (absolute reduction, -1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.1 to -0.1 percentage points; P = .04). There was no statistically significant change in adverse events (0.03%; 95% CI, -0.02% to 0.03%; P = .84) or spending on the 9 low-value services ($0.33; 95% CI, -$3.43 to $4.11).

Conclusions and relevance: In this quality improvement study, a statewide, clinician-led initiative was associated with a small but statistically significant reduction in low-value care delivery without evidence of harm. Achieving larger reductions may require combining such health system-driven efforts with additional strategies, such as payment reform and physician and hospital accountability, that discourage the use of low-value care.

Mafi JN, Bortz BA, Vangala S, Tseng CH, Russell K, Cui M

item.title: Drug Burden Index Stewardship to Deprescribe Anticholinergic or Sedative Drugs in Older Inpatients: A Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Anticholinergic and sedative medications contribute to poor clinical outcomes in older inpatients. Evidence-based deprescribing strategies are needed.

Objective: To evaluate whether an intervention bundle increases deprescribing of anticholinergic and sedative medications in older inpatients.

Design, setting, and participants: This stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial was conducted in 6 Australian public hospitals from January 2022 to July 2023. Participants were patients 65 years and older with Drug Burden Index (DBI; a measure of anticholinergic and sedative medication exposure) score greater than 0 at admission and hospitalized for 48 hours or more. Data were analyzed from October 2023 to May 2026.

Interventions: The intervention bundle had 2 components. The informational component (automated DBI score calculation displayed in the electronic medical record, deprescribing guides, patient leaflets, and education module) was present in all trial phases, although clinicians were not informed of it during the control phase. The stewardship component (study stewardship pharmacists who promoted the informational component and made patient-level deprescribing recommendations to attending teams) was delivered in the intervention phase. The informational component was promoted 1 to 2 times monthly during the sustainability phase.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with 1 or more DBI-contributing medications deprescribed (ceased or dose reduced) at discharge compared with admission. Secondary outcomes included deprescribing recommendations in discharge summaries and in-hospital adverse events.

Results: Among 4827 included patients, 2798 (58.0%) were female, and the median (IQR) age was 83.0 (76.0-88.0) years. The proportion of patients with 1 or more DBI-contributing medications deprescribed was 38.1% (788 of 2069) in the control phase, 41.4% (326 of 788) in the intervention phase, and 37.0% (729 of 1970) in the sustainability phase. The adjusted absolute difference (aAD) between intervention and control was 5.3 percentage points (95% CI, 0.1-10.6), smaller than hypothesized. Deprescribing was predominantly by cessation; in the intervention phase, 256 of 788 patients (32.5%) had 1 or more DBI-contributing medications ceased, 91 (11.5%) had 1 or more doses reduced, and 21 (2.7%) had both. The aAD between the sustainability and intervention phase estimates was -5.3 percentage points (95% CI, -10.9 to 0.3). Deprescribing recommendations in discharge summaries were more prevalent in the intervention (176 of 751 admissions [23.4%]) than the control phase (287 of 1968 admissions [14.6%]; aAD, 10.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.0-15.1) and were lower in the sustainability phase (362 of 1910 [19.0%]; aAD, -4.0 percentage points; 95% CI, -8.7 to 0.8). In-hospital adverse events were similar across phases.

Conclusions and relevance: In this stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial, the intervention bundle increased deprescribing less than hypothesized, and the increase was not sustained once the stewardship component ended.

Trial registration: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry: ACTRN12622000374763.

Fujita K, Masnoon N, Gnjidic D, Etherton-Beer C, Reeve E, Magin P
